The US House of Representatives has voted to make daylight saving time permanent by passing the Sunshine Protection Act on Tuesday.

With a 308-117 vote, members of both parties approved the bill, which would remove the need for Americans to change their clocks twice a year and put the US under time currently observed between March and November - known as permanent standard time.

Republican Scott DesJarlais, who presided over the vote, played a clip of The Beatles' Here Comes the Sun on his phone during the final count

The time-change issue has been gaining bipartisan support for years, with President Donald Trump pledging to end clock changes after he returned to the White House.

Will US really stop changing its clocks twice a year?

Republican Representative Vern Buchanan of Florida, who introduced the bill in January 2025, said on Tuesday that clock changes disrupt schedules "for no good reason".

Now that the House has passed the legislation, the Senate could soon take up its version of the bill. Florida Republican Rick Scott introduced an identical piece of legislation, also called the Sunshine Protection Act, in January 2025.

Since World War One, the US has set its clocks forward during the summer to have more daylight in the afternoon and to conserve electricity. The time-change is known as Daylight Saving Time (DST). Clocks roll back in the autumn each year to then follow standard time.

DST, which also helped conserve fuel during the first world war, was unpopular with farmers and was repealed after the war. It returned during World War Two, and legislation standardising clock-changing across the country passed in 1966, although some states, including Hawaii and Arizona, and US territories Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, have opted out.

But critics of permanent DST have noted that it would lead to darker  winter mornings, which could make driving conditions more hazardous for those on the road in early hours.

A decades-old debate over America’s clocks is headed back to Congress as lawmakers prepare to consider whether daylight saving time should be made permanent nationwide.

The U.S. House is expected to vote on the Sunshine Protection Act, a proposal that would end the twice-yearly clock changes and keep daylight saving time in effect year-round.

The legislation previously cleared the Senate in 2022 but stalled before reaching a vote in the House.

The House Energy and Commerce Committee recently advanced the measure with overwhelming support, setting the stage for a possible vote. If approved, the measure could affect when Americans see sunrise and sunset throughout the year.

The Sunshine Protection Act would stop the annual switch between standard time and daylight saving time, meaning Americans would no longer move their clocks forward in the spring and back in the fall.

Supporters of the proposal say changing the clocks can disrupt sleep patterns and may contribute to safety concerns, including more workplace accidents and traffic crashes.

They also argue that longer evening daylight could encourage more outdoor activities and economic activity.

The current version of the bill would give states the option to remain on standard time rather than require every state to adopt permanent daylight saving time.

Alabama lawmakers have already signaled support for keeping daylight saving time year-round.

In 2021, Gov. Kay Ivey signed Senate Bill 388, which would move Alabama to permanent daylight saving time if Congress gave states the authority to make that change.

The law cannot take effect under current federal rules. Congress must first approve a nationwide change before Alabama can officially make the switch.

Not everyone supports keeping daylight saving time all year.

Critics argue the change could create problems during the winter months, especially in states where sunrise would occur much later in the morning.

Some lawmakers have raised concerns about children traveling to school before daylight.

Opponents point to the nation’s previous attempt at year-round daylight saving time in the 1970s, which ended after public complaints about dark mornings.

Alabama is among a group of states that have passed legislation or expressed support for making daylight saving time permanent if Congress approves the change.

payload.title: Yhdysvaltain edustajainhuone hyväksyi pysyvän kesäajan
payload.summary: Edustajainhuone hyväksyi kellojen siirtämisen lopettavan lakiesityksen äänin 308–117. Pysyvä kesäaika edellyttää vielä senaatin käsittelyä.
payload.content:
Yhdysvaltain edustajainhuone hyväksyi tiistaina Sunshine Protection Act -lakiesityksen, joka tekisi kesäajasta pysyvän koko maassa ja lopettaisi kellojen siirtämisen kahdesti vuodessa. Esitys eteni äänin 308–117 sekä republikaanien että demokraattien tuella. Päätös ei kuitenkaan muuta käytäntöä vielä, sillä lakiesitys tarvitsee seuraavaksi senaatin käsittelyn.

## Kellojen siirtäminen loppuisi

Lakiesityksen mukaan Yhdysvalloissa jäisi ympärivuotisesti voimaan aika, jota noudatetaan nykyisin maaliskuun ja marraskuun välisenä aikana. Amerikkalaiset eivät enää siirtäisi kellojaan keväällä tuntia eteenpäin eivätkä syksyllä takaisin normaaliaikaan. Muutos vaikuttaisi siihen, mihin aikaan aurinko nousee ja laskee eri vuodenaikoina.

Kellojen siirtämisestä on kiistelty Yhdysvalloissa vuosikymmeniä. Pysyvää kesäaikaa koskeva esitys hyväksyttiin senaatissa jo vuonna 2022, mutta se pysähtyi tuolloin ennen edustajainhuoneen äänestystä. Tällä kertaa edustajainhuoneen energia- ja kauppavaliokunta puolsi esityksen etenemistä vahvalla tuella ennen täysistunnon äänestystä.

Presidentti Donald Trump on tukenut kellojen siirtämisen lopettamista ja lupasi palattuaan Valkoiseen taloon edistää muutosta. Asia on saanut vuosien mittaan kannatusta molemmissa pääpuolueissa. Äänestystä johtanut republikaaniedustaja Scott DesJarlais soitti loppulaskennan aikana puhelimestaan katkelman The Beatlesin Here Comes the Sun -kappaleesta.

## Pimeät talviaamut herättävät vastustusta

Pysyvän kesäajan arvostelijat varoittavat, että aurinko nousisi talvikuukausina nykyistä myöhemmin etenkin joissakin osavaltioissa. Osa lainsäätäjistä on nostanut esiin koululaisten turvallisuuden, sillä lapset voisivat joutua kulkemaan kouluun ennen päivän valkenemista. Vastustajat muistuttavat myös Yhdysvaltain 1970-luvulla tekemästä ympärivuotisen kesäajan kokeilusta, joka päättyi pimeitä aamuja koskeneiden valitusten jälkeen.

Alabama kuuluu osavaltioihin, jotka ovat hyväksyneet pysyvää kesäaikaa tukevia lakeja tai ilmaisseet kannattavansa muutosta, jos kongressi hyväksyy sen valtakunnallisesti. Edustajainhuoneen äänestys oli lakihankkeen seuraava askel, mutta hyväksyntä ei yksin lopeta kellojen siirtämistä. Senaatin on vielä käsiteltävä esitys, eikä käsittelyn aikataulusta kerrottu lähteissä. Siihen asti amerikkalaiset jatkavat kellojen siirtämistä keväällä ja syksyllä nykyiseen tapaan.
summary_bullets: Edustajainhuone hyväksyi pysyvää kesäaikaa koskevan esityksen äänin 308–117.
Muutos lopettaisi kellojen siirtämisen keväällä ja syksyllä.
Esitys tarvitsee vielä senaatin käsittelyn ennen kuin käytäntö voi muuttua.

The House of Representatives passed a Trump-backed bill that would end decades of Americans having to reset their clocks twice a year.

The US House of Representatives has voted to make daylight saving time permanent by passing the Sunshine Protection Act on Tuesday. With a 308-117 vote, members of both parties approved the bill, which would remove the need for Americans to change their clocks twice a year and put the US under time currently observed between March and November - known as permanent standard time. Republican Scott DesJarlais, who presided over the vote, played a clip of The Beatles' Here Comes the Sun on his phone during the final count The time-change issue has been gaining bipartisan support for years, with President Donald Trump pledging to end clock changes after he returned to the White House. Will US really stop changing its clocks twice a year?

A decades-old debate over America’s clocks is headed back to Congress as lawmakers prepare to consider whether daylight saving time should be made permanent nationwide. The U.S. House is expected to vote on the Sunshine Protection Act, a proposal that would end the twice-yearly clock changes and keep daylight saving time in effect year-round. The legislation previously cleared the Senate in 2022 but stalled before reaching a vote in the House. The House Energy and Commerce Committee recently advanced the measure with overwhelming support, setting the stage for a possible vote. If approved, the measure could affect when Americans see sunrise and sunset throughout the year. The Sunshine Protection Act would stop the annual switch between standard time and daylight saving time, meaning Americans would no longer move their clocks forward in the spring and back in the fall.

Critics argue the change could create problems during the winter months, especially in states where sunrise would occur much later in the morning. Some lawmakers have raised concerns about children traveling to school before daylight. Opponents point to the nation’s previous attempt at year-round daylight saving time in the 1970s, which ended after public complaints about dark mornings. Alabama is among a group of states that have passed legislation or expressed support for making daylight saving time permanent if Congress approves the change.
